“Whoever wrote this,” snarls a policeman about Katurian’s prose, “is a sick, f***ing, scummy c***.” Ha ha ha, went perhaps five people in the audience. Never before, when seeing a character suffocated, have I felt such sharp envy.
Sharply funny, gasp-inducing and richly thought-provoking, this is bold, uncompromising drama that startlingly interrogates its own artistic medium.
Dunster’s impeccable directing means the audience can’t help but remain gripped throughout.
If this play is a manifesto of provocation, which proves its point about censorship by pushing its ideas to the limit, then it certainly succeeds — and then some.
It doesn’t seem quite the winner 2003 thought it.
On this showing, it emerges as a clever, resilient piece of writing but less profound than perhaps it hopes to be.

Though quite an achievement, in many places the subject matter is uniquely discomforting and many of the chuckles emanating from audience members seemed born of a determination to be amused despite the underlying darkness and despair inherent in the story.

A fascinating show from start to finish, The Pillowman is undoubtedly one of the best plays of the year.
Matthew Dunster’s production of The Pillowman, is a masterpiece of dark comedy.
The Pillowman is every bit as puzzling and disturbing as I recalled from its National Theatre debut.
A wonderfully shocking experience, packed with food for thought, and not for the fainthearted.
Otherwise, it’s a sensational show that rattles the mind and stirs the soul, and will not be easily forgotten.
Dunster handles the play's complex ideas adeptly in a show that balances claustrophobic suspense with provocative humour.
While inventive and well-acted, the play remains opaque and open to interpretation.
But in this meticulous formaldehyde of one, the cleansed world is full of cracks.
The main three performances are strong nonetheless.
Allen is responsible for delivering a raft of mind-boggling monologues, proving magnificent in the role.
For a show based so heavily on imagination, this retelling lacks the emotional impact it could have achieved.

cn.t: McDonagh's dark, provocative play about storytelling and censorship divides critics in its belated West End debut. Most praise the writing's craft and relevance, though some find it dated or gratuitously shocking. Allen's performance proves polarizing.
